5.title: About Salt
5.summary: Salt is the J.P. Morgan design system, an open-source solution for building exceptional products and digital experiences in financial services and other industries.

6.title: Accordion
6.summary: For assistive technologies, the visible label on a control usually acts as the accessible name.

7.title: Accordion
7.summary: By default, Accordion is a single element the user can expand or collapse to show or hide content within a panel.

9.title: Accordion
9.summary: To organize related content within expandable groups/categories/sections.

10.title: Actionable characteristic
10.summary: Actionable tokens define the colors and styles for actionable components, making elements that can perform actions—such as buttons—distinct and easy to identify. Actionable is organized by sentiment values (accented, caution, positive, negative) and emphasis levels (bold, subtle), allowing you to convey the importance or nature of an action.

11.title: Analytical dashboard
11.summary:
An analytical dashboard enables users to analyze trends, patterns and metrics effectively. You can use this to present data in a hierarchical and intuitive manner.

The mock-ups displayed in this pattern are available as [templates](https://www.figma.com/file/O3FYUQYXLosmEuZc0T30Qo/Analytical-Dashboard-Pattern?type=design&node-id=1288-5747&mode=design&t=Pu46NKEwCeMRSjPD-0) in Figma _(J.P. Morgan employees only)_.

12.title: Announcement dialog
12.summary: An announcement dialog promotes new features and can provide users with access to onward action, such as installing version updates.

13.title: App header
13.summary: An app header is a consistently available element that sits at the top of every application interface. It contains a brand logo or mark and application-wide functionality, including navigation and utility actions.

14.title: Avatar
14.summary: Exclude decorative avatars (avatars that repeat the information already expressed by the accompanying text) from screen reader access to avoid repetition. If you're adding an avatar for decorative purposes, use aria-hidden to exclude its label from the screen reader.

15.title: Avatar
15.summary: You can pass an image as the avatar image using the src prop.

17.title: Avatar
17.summary: To visually represent a person, group, entity or communication channel. The same image, initials, or placeholder image should appear for a given object instance throughout the experience.

18.title: Badge
18.summary: When you've attached a badge to a child component, and that component receives focus, ensure the focusable element has an aria-label or aria-labelledby attribute that describes the badge, such as "9 notifications." - When the user navigates to an inline badge, the screen reader automatically announces the contents of the badge. Use aria-label to provide more context to the badge contents if needed.

19.title: Badge
19.summary: The Badge is anchored to the top-right corner when attached to a child component such as a button. As the number of alphanumeric characters increases, the badge width expands but stays in the same place.

21.title: Badge
21.summary: If a numeric annotation exceeds the max value passed as a prop, there will be a plus (+) after the max value stated. If you don't pass a max value to the component, it will truncate the value after three digits displaying 999+ for any values over 999.

22.title: Banner
22.summary: Check and test any focusable elements included in the banner content.

23.title: Banner
23.summary: The static banner displays information to the user, has no interactive elements, and is nonfunctional.

25.title: Banner
25.summary: Always position the banner component in the main content area or in the related container component. It should sit directly below the navigation and span the page or container horizontally.

26.title: Border layout
26.summary: When building a page layout, apply semantic HTML. This means using the correct HTML elements for their intended purpose as much as possible.

27.title: Border layout
27.summary: You can set BorderLayout to display five regions: North, East, South, West and Center. You must display at least one region alongside the Center region in the layout.

29.title: Border layout
29.summary: To manage the top-level layout of your application, or page, with at least one additional region alongside the main content area (e.g., for navigation or a footer).

30.title: Border style
30.summary: The border style foundation provides a standardized set of design tokens to ensure consistent border styles across all components and patterns.

31.title: Breadcrumbs
31.summary: Breadcrumbs are a secondary navigation pattern that helps users keep track of their current location within a hierarchy. It provides a space-efficient means of allowing quick navigation to previous levels.

32.title: Breakpoints
32.summary: Responsive design utilizes breakpoints to adapt UI layouts and optimize presentation of information across different application resolutions and orientations. This approach enhances user experience by ensuring content remains readable and accessible.

33.title: Button
33.summary: When a button has both an icon and text, use aria-hidden on the icon so that screen readers don't announce its text.

34.title: Button
34.summary: The accented button is the main button set for your UI. It is typically used for the core actions in your workflow. Three different appearances are available based on the prominence required for the actions.

36.title: Button
36.summary: Keep the text description short, ideally one to three words and no more than five. If you’re including an icon with the text, use no more than three words.

37.title: Button bar
37.summary: A button bar displays possible actions for users to take when they reach the end of a task. You can use it to provide consistent presentation of button types and orders within pages or dialogs across your applications.

38.title: Calendar
38.summary: The Calendar component is typically not used on its own but is composed with other components to build more user-friendly components such as DatePicker.

39.title: Calendar
39.summary: When the selectionVariant prop is set to "single", the Calendar component allows users to select only a single date, providing a straightforward and focused date selection experience.

41.title: Calendar
41.summary: To use the Calendar component, compose it with the provided children.

42.title: Card
42.summary: To meet accessibility standards, the boundaries of a user interface component are only subject to the 3:1 contrast minimum if they serve to identify the components purpose.

43.title: Card
43.summary: By default, the card component does not have any interactive or focusable elements.

45.title: Card
45.summary: Cards may include text, images, or interactive elements. Make sure the content aligns with your use case, keeping it clear and easy to read. Avoid overcrowding cards with excessive content, actions, or links embedded in the text.

46.title: Carousel
46.summary: Avoid using infographics, maps, or charts as images, and do not use images of text.

47.title: Carousel
47.summary: Carousel is a pre-defined composition of Salt components that uses the Embla API.

49.title: Carousel
49.summary: Carousels offer two types of navigation, sequential and non-sequential.

50.title: Categorical colors
50.summary: Salt’s categorical palette is designed for data visualization and components that represent distinct categories, featuring 20 unique colors and their corresponding ramps.

51.title: Category characteristic
51.summary: Category tokens provide a palette of distinct colors for differentiating groups within your interface, such as in data visualizations or components that support content grouping. While the colors themselves do not imply meaning, meaning can be associated to each category within the context of your application.

52.title: Chart
52.summary: Highcharts provides an accessibility module that enhances the accessibility of charts.

53.title: Chart
53.summary: To ensure the presentation is accessible, line or fill patterns can be applied to the chart (see Patterns and Fills for details). Use the "Show patterns" switch to toggle patterns.

55.title: Chart
55.summary: Install the following dependencies: - highcharts - version 10.2.0 specifically, or version 11+ - highcharts-react-official - @salt-ds/highcharts-theme

56.title: Chart accessibility
56.summary: Charts rely on visual elements to make complex data easier to understand, so it’s essential they are accessible to everyone. Ground your chart design and implementation in the WCAG POUR principles: - **Perceivable**: Text equivalents (caption, summary), accessible data table, sufficient contrast, labels/patterns/markers instead of color alone.

57.title: Chart anatomy
57.summary: Understanding the principles of chart anatomy is important to learning how the different parts of Salt charts work.

58.title: Chart types
58.summary: Data visualization presents information in a visual form that’s easy to understand. When applied to dense and complex datasets, it aids in highlighting trends and patterns.

59.title: Checkbox
59.summary: If you're using a checkbox without a text description, pass an aria-label to the checkbox that describes its purpose.

60.title: Checkbox
60.summary: A single checkbox can be either selected or deselected.

62.title: Checkbox
62.summary: To present an independent choice that the user can select or deselect.

63.title: Collapsible
63.summary: If focus is above the collapsible trigger, Tab moves focus to the trigger.

64.title: Collapsible
64.summary: Collapsible is a component that allows you to show or hide content with a click. It can be used to create expandable sections in your UI.

66.title: Collapsible
66.summary: To import Collapsible and related components from the core Salt package, use:

67.title: Color and pattern
67.summary: Color is a valuable tool that helps effectively present data in your visualization. Using color correctly guides users’ attention and supports their understanding and interpretation of data.

68.title: Combo box
68.summary: If the combo box is single-select and if focus is above the combo box, Tab sets focus on the component. When focused, combo box has a visible text cursor and the list is opened.

69.title: Combo box
69.summary: By default, a single item can be selected from the combo box options. The selected option is displayed in the input field.

71.title: Combo box
71.summary: To display and select from a list of 10 or more options that don't need to be permanently visible to the user without selecting from a dropdown menu.

72.title: Components
72.summary: Our components are built with accessibility in mind. Each one has comprehensive supporting documentation with usage guidance, examples and props.

73.title: Contact details
73.summary: Contact details display communication information for a person, company, distribution list or individual channel. This can include a name, a phone number or email address.

74.title: Container characteristic
74.summary: Container tokens define the background and structure of interface elements, helping to group related content and create visual hierarchy. Each variant—primary, secondary, and tertiary—aligns with theme background colors to support different levels of emphasis. Containers can also include borders and shadows, with shadow options provided by the Overlayable characteristic, to further distinguish and elevate content within your layout.

75.title: Content characteristic
75.summary: Content tokens define the standard foreground colors for all text and icons within Salt, ensuring clarity and consistency across your interface. Available in variants such as primary, secondary, accent, and attention, these tokens should be applied to all foreground elements unless another characteristic—like actionable—takes precedence for interactive states. Using content tokens appropriately helps maintain visual harmony and supports accessibility throughout your application.

76.title: Content status
76.summary: A content status provides information about content in a container component of an application. It remains onscreen until a situation resolves or the user takes action, making it a great tool for communication and guidance.

77.title: Country symbol
77.summary: If you're using a country symbol for decorative purposes, and the country is named in accompanying text, hide its label from screen readers to avoid repetition. To hide the label, pass aria-hidden=”true”.

78.title: Country symbol
78.summary: We include all countries and subdivisions that appear in the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 3166-1 standard. Though we use the country names, alpha-2 codes and corresponding alphabetical order from ISO, our symbols derive from whichever flag the official United Nations list provides for each country. Of the 249 countries currently in the ISO list, 193 are sovereign states with UN membership. We also include the EU symbol, due to its economic importance.

80.title: Country symbol
80.summary: To reduce the core package's bundle size, country symbols are in a separate package that you should first install using: npm install @salt-ds/countries or yarn add @salt-ds/countries

81.title: Country symbols
81.summary: Country symbols represent a specific place and are used in contexts where geographical identification is necessary. They are essentially icons that are visually indicative of a country or territory. All country symbols are available in both circle and rectangle shapes.

82.title: Cursor
82.summary: The cursor foundation controls how the cursor appears when positioned over or interacting with a component. This behavior is only relevant for web browsers and operating systems that display cursors in the user interface.

83.title: Data grid
83.summary: This package has no accessibility guidance.

84.title: Data grid
84.summary: Applies the default look when applying the Salt theme.

86.title: Data grid
86.summary: When you want to use the Salt theme with AG Grid.

87.title: Date input
87.summary: Wrap DateInputSingle and DateInputRange in FormField to provide the field with a visible label, help text, and a status message for validation feedback. This will ensure it complies with accessibility guidelines. You can find more information in the W3C form instructions.

88.title: Date input
88.summary: An uncontrolled DateInputSingle component allows users to select a single date without the need for explicit state management in the parent component. The component internally manages the date value, making it ideal for simple forms where the date input does not need to be programmatically controlled or monitored.

90.title: Date input
90.summary: To avoid misleading users, set the width of the input to correlate with the length of the expected answer. For example, an input for a three-digit value shouldn't be wide enough to accommodate a sentence worth of characters. See forms pattern for more information on layout.

91.title: Date picker
91.summary: Wrap DatePicker in FormField to provide the field with a visible label, help text, and a status message for validation feedback. This will ensure it complies with accessibility guidelines. You can find more information in the W3C form instructions.

92.title: Date picker
92.summary: All date components requires LocalizationProvider to be set up in your application.

94.title: Date picker
94.summary: DatePicker provides a context to the children contained within it and a composable API that enables you to create your own date picker controls.

95.title: Density
95.summary: Density relates to the amount of content that can fit on a screen based on the size and spacing of components. When building a product with Salt, select the density that best suits your use case. All components, spacing, and typographic elements will align and remain proportionate regardless of the density you choose.

96.title: Design tokens
96.summary: Salt styles its components and patterns using design tokens. Design tokens are name and value pairings that capture small, repeatable design choices—such as colors, fonts, and spacing—and are essential for storing key style attributes in a design system. They help maintain consistency across platforms and applications, making it easier to update and maintain a cohesive look throughout your products.

97.title: Designing with Salt Figma libraries
97.summary: Salt provides a comprehensive set of components and styles, which include themes, typography, color palettes, iconography and more. Designers can use the components as they are, out of the box, or adapt them to suit the needs of a business or application.

98.title: Developing with Salt
98.summary: Learn how to use Salt's UI components in your React web applications.

99.title: Dialog
99.summary: Provide an accessible name for dialogs by using the visible DialogHeader (recommended) or, if design constraints prevent this, apply an aria-label attribute directly to the Dialog to meet WCAG 4.1.2 requirements.

100.title: Dialog
100.summary: The dialog displays with a header, content area, and action bar. The component is modal, meaning it prevents interaction with the rest of the UI while open and must be addressed by clicking one of the action buttons or dismissing with the close button in DialogHeader. If the content of the dialog extends beyond the end of the screen, the DialogContent area will become scrollable.

102.title: Dialog
102.summary: Dialogs are interruptive by nature and should be used sparingly. Use dialogs to present or gather critical information that requires immediate action, whether it’s directly or indirectly part of the user’s current task. For example, a warning dialog that appears when a document is closed without being saved—and asks how the user wishes to proceed—is indirectly related to the user’s task.

103.title: Divider
103.summary: Divider has a role of separator and is sometimes announced by screen readers as "Horizontal Splitter". If you're adding a divider for decorative purposes, pass aria-hidden="true" to make screen readers skip it.

104.title: Divider
104.summary: Divider has three variants: primary, secondary and tertiary. The default variant is primary. You can use the variant prop to change

106.title: Divider
106.summary: To provide visual separation between elements, regions and containers.

107.title: Drawer
107.summary: If focus is on the trigger element, this action activates the element and opens the drawer. Focus doesn't leave the drawer.

108.title: Drawer
108.summary: By default, a drawer anchors to the left edge of the screen and has variant="primary".

110.title: Drawer
110.summary: Drawers cover the entire height of the viewport and are always modal. This means that the content behind them is inert and can't be interacted with. A Scrim is used to visually obscure the content behind the drawer.

111.title: Dropdown
111.summary: If focus is above the dropdown, Tab sets focus on the component. When focused, dropdown has a visible text cursor and the list is opened.

112.title: Dropdown
112.summary: Users can select a single item from the dropdown options.

114.title: Dropdown
114.summary: When a user needs the ability to choose one value from a set of five to 10 options.

115.title: Duration
115.summary: Duration represents the time between a user performing an action and the system giving feedback. It’s essential to indicate to users that something is happening when they interact with an element. Consistency in timing provides user comfort and can increase trust in a system. The duration should match the significance of the animated element or information.

116.title: Editable characteristic
116.summary: Editable tokens specify the colors and styles for components that support data entry and modification. This characteristic is used for input controls like text fields, where users can write or edit information. Editable tokens ensure that these components are visually distinct and easy to identify, often accompanied by labels to guide user interaction and support clear, accessible data entry.

117.title: Extended styling
117.summary: Salt provides you with options which enable you to customize your UI for specific use cases, whilst keeping everything consistent and maintainable. You can adjust densities, switch themes, and choose between light and dark modes. Most components offer props that help to establish clear hierarchy or alter prominence, with predefined variants and appearances to fit different situations. There are also semantic color options for sentiment, status, and categories—giving you plenty of flexibility without needing to override.

118.title: Feedback
118.summary: We appreciate your thoughts and feedback on any content in the Salt foundations. Please contact us if you have any comments or questions.

119.title: Feedback
119.summary: If you need to expand the pattern or share feedback with us, please contact the team.

120.title: File drop zone
120.summary: Tab sets focus to the **'Browse files'** button. If focus is in the file drop zone, Tab sets focus to the next focusable component in the tab order.

121.title: File drop zone
121.summary: This component allows users to upload files they've selected from the native file browser interface or dragged-and-dropped. The component automatically uploads the files to your web application.

123.title: File drop zone
123.summary: To enable users to upload single or multiple files from a native file browser.

124.title: File upload
124.summary: A file upload allows users to transfer one or multiple files from an external source to the web application. This pattern is commonly embedded in forms or as a standalone element.

125.title: Flex layout
125.summary: When building a layout for part of a page using FlexLayout, apply semantic HTML. This means using the correct HTML elements for their intended purpose as much as possible.

126.title: Flex layout
126.summary: By default, FlexLayout displays items along the horizontal axis in a row, aligned to the start of the container. The dimensions of the layout (height or width) are driven by the items contained within it.

128.title: Flex layout
128.summary: When a complex layout cannot first be achieved using flow, stack and split layouts. However, if you are very familiar with CSS Flexbox, you may choose to use a flex layout from the start.

129.title: Flow layout
129.summary: When building a sub-section of a page using a flow layout, apply semantic HTML, This means using the correct HTML elements for their intended purpose as much as possible.

130.title: Flow layout
130.summary: A flow layout displays items in a row that will responsively wrap onto a new line.

132.title: Flow layout
132.summary: To build responsive layouts that wrap across multiple rows when there isn't enough space in the viewport.

133.title: Form field
133.summary: All keyboard interactions are supplied by the underlying wrapped components, rather than the FormField component.

134.title: Form field
134.summary: All examples demonstrate Salt form controls inside the form field, including Input, Checkbox and RadioButton. These components are available as part of the Salt component library in addition to FormField.

136.title: Form field
136.summary: We highly recommend using the FormFieldLabel and FormFieldHelperText components within the form field to provide your form elements with the descriptive label and validation feedback required to ensure ADA compliance.

137.title: Forms
137.summary: A form allows you to capture data, gather opinions and receive information in a consistent format. This pattern provides guidelines for creating forms that are flexible to business domain, user experience and channel.

138.title: Foundations
138.summary: Foundations are the fundamental principles that guide the creation of a cohesive design language, enabling you to build products that are easy to use and visually appealing.

139.title: Get started
139.summary: Follow our step-by-step guides to design and develop accessible, responsive, best-in-class user experiences with Salt.

140.title: Glossary
140.summary: Learn what technical terms for design and development mean specifically in the context of Salt. Note that the order of this glossary of definitions is purposefully not alphabetical but is sequenced according to the Salt site navigation, so that related terms appear next to similar concepts.

141.title: Grid layout
141.summary: When building a page layout, apply semantic HTML. This means using the correct HTML elements for their intended purpose as much as possible.

142.title: Grid layout
142.summary: GridLayout defaults to a 12-column grid with one row.

144.title: Grid layout
144.summary: When it's best to display your content using a configurable number of columns and rows, such as a form or a dashboard.

145.title: Header block
145.summary: Header block is a standardized header for container components and application regions, used to display various text elements depending on scenarios. Headings can also display accent and status to highlight messaging.

146.title: How to read semantic tokens
146.summary: Salt organizes semantic tokens within the characteristic layer, allowing components and patterns to reference them directly. Understanding semantic characteristics involves learning how to interpret token names, making it easier to find and apply the right token in both design and code.

147.title: Icon
147.summary: Exclude decorative icons (icons that repeat the information already expressed by the accompanied text) from screen reader access to avoid repetition. If you're adding an icon for decorative purposes, pass aria-hidden=”true” to exclude its label from the screen reader.

148.title: Icon
148.summary: You should individually import and use from the @salt-ds/icons package.

150.title: Icon
150.summary: To aid recognition and help users make choices by providing context (e.g., an office phone number vs cell phone number in contact information).

151.title: Icons
151.summary: Icons are simplified visual representations of a specific action, object or concept.

152.title: Indication
152.summary: The indication pattern provides a starting point for designers to apply common indication scenarios, with consideration for color, iconography and recommended labeling guidelines.

153.title: Input
153.summary: Wrap Input in FormField to provide the field with a visible label, help text, and a status message for validation feedback. This will ensure it complies with accessibility guidelines. You can find more information in the W3C form instructions.

154.title: Input
154.summary: Input is a single-line text field that accepts user input. It can be used in forms, search bars, or anywhere you need to capture user input.

156.title: Input
156.summary: To avoid misleading users, set the width to correlate to the length of the answer you’re expecting. For example, an input for a three-digit value shouldn't be wide enough to accommodate a sentence worth of characters. See forms pattern for more information on layout.

157.title: International address form
157.summary:
An international address form gives users a set of form fields to input address information for specific countries. The form displays relevant fields for a user-selected location.

The pattern aims to accommodate users worldwide, but your team may be able to take further steps that fall outside its scope. For example, check with your tech partners if it's possible to detect user location and automatically adjust the form.

Future versions of this pattern will cover the use of APIs, autocompletion and enhanced support for more locations.

158.title: International phone number
158.summary:
An international phone number input gives users a set of form fields to input phone number information for specific countries.

The pattern is a form that displays a relevant phone number field for a user-selected location. You can use it to provide consistent design when implementing International Phone Number Input interactions across your applications.

We provide design guidance on how you can use Salt form control components to achieve the pattern. Your team can take further steps that fall outside its scope. For example, check with your tech partners if it’s possible to autodetect user location using data that can support auto-generating number placeholders. You can also check if it's possible to save the entered number when the user changes the country.

159.title: JPM brand characteristic tokens
159.summary: Accent highlights key elements by applying a theme's dominant color, helping important components—like active tabs or headings—stand out and draw attention.

160.title: JPM brand colors
160.summary: These are the JPM brand theme colors, approved for digital use by the brand team. The palette supports clear communication, visual hierarchy, and product differentiation, while ensuring a cohesive and accessible experience across Salt applications.

161.title: Kbd
161.summary: Screen readers will announce Kbd content as plain text.

162.title: Kbd
162.summary: Kbd supports multiple background color variants: primary, secondary, and tertiary. The primary variant is set by default. These variants help match different UI backgrounds and provide varying levels of visual emphasis, depending on how important the shortcuts are in a given scenario.

164.title: Kbd
164.summary: To display keyboard shortcuts: Use Kbd to visually highlight keyboard keys or combinations (e.g., "Ctrl + S") in documentation.

165.title: Keyboard shortcuts
165.summary: Keyboard shortcuts allow users to execute actions, that are usually performed with a mouse or trackpad, using a keyboard. They increase the efficiency and productivity of users who primarily rely on their keyboard when interacting with applications.

166.title: Layout grid
166.summary: A layout grid provides a consistent structure for Salt user interfaces, organizing content into columns separated by gutters and framed by margins. The grid adapts to different screen sizes, with column number and width changing by density and breakpoint. This ensures layouts remain clear, balanced, and accessible across devices.

167.title: Legacy (UITK) characteristics tokens
167.summary: Accent highlights key elements by applying a theme's dominant color, helping important components—like active tabs or headings—stand out and draw attention.

168.title: Legacy (UITK) colors
168.summary: Salt recommends using the JPM brand theme for your product, as the legacy (UITK) color palette is not aligned with current brand standards and may present accessibility challenges. The legacy palette is provided primarily to support migration from UI Toolkit to Salt, and should only be used when necessary for compatibility.

169.title: Link
169.summary: Screen reader users will use the Tab key to jump from link to link or pull up a list of links on a page. Avoid using the same link text to link to different content and ensure that links make sense out of context.

170.title: Link
170.summary: By default, a link will only navigate the user within the same tab, replacing the page where the user followed the link.

172.title: Link
172.summary: To provide navigation to a page on the same or different site.

173.title: List box
173.summary: If focus is above the list, Tab moves focus to one of the following options depending on previous user interaction: - The last selected option - The first option in the list If focus is below the list, this action moves focus to one of the following options depending on previous user interaction: - The last selected option - The last option in the list When focus is on an option, this action selects the option and if the list box is single-select deselects the previously selected option, if any.

174.title: List box
174.summary: The default list allows a user to make a single selection from the options available.

176.title: List box
176.summary: To present a set of selectable options that allow users to make a choice for an onward action, such as filtering a data grid, selecting a country or assigning a task.

177.title: List builder
177.summary: A list builder allows users to create a bespoke list of items from an original list, also known as a pick list, adding or removing items as required. Users can filter the items by using the filter input field.

178.title: List filtering
178.summary: When searching through a list, a filter enables users to specify criteria and only show relevant options. This pattern introduces the filter behavior of Salt components where a list is used.

179.title: Localization provider
179.summary: This component has no accessibility guidance.

180.title: Localization provider
180.summary: To integrate your date framework with Salt components and enable support for locales or timezones, defining a date adapter is essential. Salt provides date adapters for the most popular date frameworks, which you can extend or use as a foundation to create your own custom adapter.

182.title: Localization provider
182.summary: Wrap your application with typically one LocalizationProvider to define the date adapter for date based controls.

183.title: Menu
183.summary: If focus is on a menu item, Tab closes the menu and moves focus to the next focusable element in the tab order.

184.title: Menu
184.summary: Clicking on the menu trigger will display a list of actions that the user can take.

186.title: Menu
186.summary: Menu items should relate to the interactive element or interaction that triggers the menu.

187.title: Menu button
187.summary: A menu button expands to reveal numerous contextual options when there's limited space to display them. The items within the menu are often less frequently used and don't require constant display within the interface.

188.title: Metric
188.summary: A metric displays an important number value prominently. You can add indicators or labels to help provide context to the presented value.

189.title: Modes
189.summary: Modes enable the color palette to change from light to dark, providing the flexibility to choose an option that best fits a preference or need. Choosing a suitable mode can improve accessibility, reduce eye strain in low-light conditions and increase reading speed.

190.title: Multiline input
190.summary: Wrap MultilineInput in FormField to provide the field with a visible label, help text and a status message for validation feedback. This will ensure it complies with accessibility guidelines. You can find more information in the W3C form instructions.

191.title: Multiline input
191.summary: MultilineInput is a text input field that allows the user to enter multiple lines of text. Values entered into the multiline input wrap based on the width of the component. By default, the component presents three rows of text at a time.

193.title: Multiline input
193.summary: Use a multiline input when asking a user a subjective question and the length of their answer is unknown. The input can give them plenty of space to answer the question and review the answer. If you can take an educated guess at the possible length of their answer, set the height accordingly—see the "Number of rows" example.

194.title: Navigable characteristic
194.summary: The Navigable characteristic defines the colors and styles for components that support navigation, such as Tabs, Vertical Navigation or Navigation Item. These components enable users to switch between sections, pages, or data sets and change context easily. The tokens highlighted in this guide ensure navigation elements are visually clear and consistent, making it easy for users to move through different parts of the interface.

195.title: Navigation
195.summary: A navigation provides users with a structured and intuitive way to go to different pages, sections or features of your website or application. It tells users where they are at all times and ensures they can easily get to where they need to go. Use this pattern to provide consistency that helps users navigate your website or application easily and efficiently.

196.title: Navigation item
196.summary: Tab moves focus into the first navigation item in the vertical group. Sets focus to the entire component.

197.title: Navigation item
197.summary: Use horizontal navigation items within a horizontal group to establish a consistent and easily accessible pathway for users, while conserving valuable screen estate. This will allow users to easily scan and identify navigation options in a seamless user experience.

199.title: Navigation item
199.summary: For further details on how to use the component to provide navigation, see the navigation pattern

200.title: Number input
200.summary: Wrap NumberInput in FormField to provide the field with a visible label, help text and a status message for validation feedback. This will ensure it complies with accessibility guidelines. You can find more information in the W3C form instructions.

201.title: Number input
201.summary: The NumberInput has a default increment step of 1, which is adjustable via the step prop for precise value changes. For larger adjustments, users can hold the Shift key while using the arrow keys to apply a stepMultiplier, a prop that defaults to 2.

203.title: Number input
203.summary: To avoid misleading users, set the width to correlate to the length of the value you’re expecting. For example, an input for a three-digit value shouldn't be wide enough to accommodate a sentence worth of characters. See forms pattern for more information on layout.

204.title: Overlay
204.summary: Users expose an overlay using a focusable UI element, such as a button. On button activation by either the Enter or Space keys, focus enters the overlay.

205.title: Overlay
205.summary: The basic overlay component allows the user to expose and interact with supplemental information. The overlay remains persistent until the user dismisses it.

207.title: Overlay
207.summary: Interaction with the content in an overlay is typically constrained, as richer interactions/workflows should occur within a separate UI mechanism (such as a new page, Dialog or Drawer).

208.title: Overlayable characteristic
208.summary: Overlayable tokens define translucent styles for shadows and scrims, as well as neutral overlay layers that highlight hovered, selected, or highlighted items without masking underlying colors. This ensures that other visual cues—like zebra striping, validation states, or sentiments—remain visible and relevant. All overlayable tokens are translucent to maintain clarity across different states.

209.title: Overview
209.summary: Salt layouts are a special category of components designed to manage the overall structure and arrangement of user interface elements, rather than providing visual UI elements themselves. Layouts are responsible for organizing how other components are positioned and flow within an application or page.

210.title: Pagination
210.summary: Tab moves focus into the pagination component, setting focus to the first focusable element.

211.title: Pagination
211.summary: Use the default component to navigate a small number of pages. The user can navigate in single page increments or jump directly to a page in a set range.

213.title: Pagination
213.summary: Position the component where it’s most appropriate for your content length. On longer pages, for example, display the component both above and below content. Placing it below the content may cause frustration and excessive scrolling, and the user may not see it if it's positioned only at the top.

214.title: Panel
214.summary: This component has no accessibility guidance.

215.title: Panel
215.summary: When using panels together, use the primary variant as the background for the most important content that you want the user to focus on first.

217.title: Panel
217.summary: Pick the background that reflects the level of importance of the content (primary or secondary), which will drive the types of components displayed in the panel.

218.title: Parent-child layout
218.summary: When building a subsection of a page using ParentChildLayout, apply semantic HTML. This means using the correct HTML elements for their intended purpose as much as possible.

219.title: Parent-child layout
219.summary: A parent-child layout displays the parent component to the left and child component to the right.

221.title: Parent-child layout
221.summary: To organize content into two areas: a larger area, and a smaller area that controls the larger area.

222.title: Patterns
222.summary: Salt is a pattern-driven system. This means we provide a set of simple, high-quality, context-agnostic components and show you how to put them together in different ways, as “patterns”, to solve a specific business problem.

223.title: Pill
223.summary: When focus is on the pill, this action activates it.

224.title: Pill
224.summary: Pills are often used for quick actions such as choosing an auto-generated response to a message or reserving a seat in a room.

226.title: Pill
226.summary: To organize selections that don’t necessarily belong to the same category or need to be arranged in a certain way.

227.title: Preferences dialog
227.summary: A preferences dialog allows you to display, group and navigate application preferences within a responsive modal dialog window. This pattern introduces guidelines to make the preferences dialog consistent and usable.

228.title: Progress
228.summary: Improve accessibility by customizing the aria-label prop to provide additional context about what is loading. For example:

229.title: Progress
229.summary: Use linear or circular depending on the context, layout and functionality of an application. Use the same indicator for the same type of process to ensure consistency.

231.title: Progress
231.summary: When it’s possible to determine the length of time remaining for a task or operation to complete. This will reassure the user that it is being processed.

232.title: Radio button
232.summary: Tab moves focus to the checked radio button in the radio button group.

233.title: Radio button
233.summary: Radio button groups allow users to select one or more values from a given set of choices. You can align them horizontally or vertically.

235.title: Radio button
235.summary: When you have fewer than five options and only single selection is necessary.

236.title: Range date picker
236.summary: Wrap DatePicker in FormField to provide the field with a visible label, help text, and a status message for validation feedback. This will ensure it complies with accessibility guidelines. You can find more information in the W3C form instructions.

237.title: Range date picker
237.summary: All date components requires LocalizationProvider to be set up in your application.

239.title: Range date picker
239.summary: DatePicker provides a context to the children contained within it and a composable API that enables you to create your own date picker controls.

240.title: Range slider
240.summary: If focus is outside the RangeSlider, moves focus to the RangeSlider indicator within the tabbing order.

241.title: Range slider
241.summary: Selection of an interval of values from a RangeSlider track. A tooltip displays the value of the RangeSlider's "thumbs" when a thumb is focused or hovered.

243.title: Range slider
243.summary: When selecting a range of numeric values or relative scale.

244.title: Rating
244.summary: Tab moves focus into the rating component. Focus is set to the selected rating item.

245.title: Rating
245.summary: By default, the Rating displays five increments, as stars, from which users can select a rating.

247.title: Rating
247.summary: When you have to provide feedback or indicate your level of satisfaction with a product, service, or experience.

248.title: Roadmap
248.summary: We track all our work using GitHub issues so if you see an issue that you're interested in please leave an 👍.

249.title: Salt Design System
249.summary: Salt is J.P. Morgan's open-source design system, providing accessible components and extensive design resources to create exceptional digital experiences across lines of business.

250.title: Salt DS Figma Component Guides
250.summary: Salt DS Figma Component Guides is a Figma library providing guidance about how to configure and customize Salt DS components.

251.title: Salt provider
251.summary: This component has no accessibility guidance.

252.title: Salt provider
252.summary: Use SaltProvider to change the theme of your application with the theme prop. You can pass in multiple theme names if needed, just like className.

254.title: Salt provider
254.summary: To import SaltProvider from the core Salt package, use:

255.title: Scrim
255.summary: This component has no accessibility guidance.

256.title: Scrim
256.summary: Use the fixed prop to make the scrim fill the viewport.

258.title: Scrim
258.summary: Place it in an application window, widget, data visualization or panel.

259.title: Search
259.summary: The Search pattern offers users an intuitive way to explore content quickly by using keywords. Search is essential to discover information in apps that support large amounts of information. This pattern supports a basic menu driven search behavior, with optional free text behavior and configurable search result items.

260.title: Segmented button group
260.summary: When using segmented button group ensure you follow the button accessibility guidance.

261.title: Segmented button group
261.summary: Group buttons of the same variant to indicate that they are related.

263.title: Segmented button group
263.summary: Within a single segmented button group, only use buttons of the same variant.

264.title: Selectable card
264.summary: A selectable card allows users to make selections by clicking anywhere within the card. It’s functionally equivalent to a form control, such as [`ToggleButton`](/salt/components/toggle-button), [`RadioButton`](/salt/components/radio-button) or [`Checkbox`](/salt/components/checkbox). You can group selectable cards to support single or multiple selection.

265.title: Selectable characteristic
265.summary: Selectable tokens specify the colors and styles for components that support user selection. This characteristic is used for elements like radio buttons, checkboxes, switches, selectable list items, and menus. Selectable ensures these components are visually clear and consistent, making it easy for users to identify and interact with options throughout an interface.

266.title: Semantic icon provider
266.summary: This component has no accessibility guidance.

267.title: Semantic icon provider
267.summary: Use the SemanticIconProvider to replace any existing icon management setup with this provider and provide any custom icon mappings as required.

269.title: Semantic icon provider
269.summary: To import SemanticIconProvider from the core Salt package, use:

270.title: Semantic use of color
270.summary: Salt uses semantic naming conventions for color, organizing tokens by their intended meaning—such as error, warning, success, or informational states. This approach ensures designs are consistent, adaptable, and accessible across themes and modes.

271.title: Sentiment characteristic
271.summary: Sentiment tokens provide visual cues that help guide users through an interface by suggesting potential outcomes and evoking specific feelings. Each sentiment—accented, neutral, positive, negative, and caution—can be used to reinforce meaning, highlight important elements, or influence user perception. By applying sentiment tokens thoughtfully, you create interfaces that are more intuitive, engaging, and emotionally resonant for users.

272.title: Separable characteristic
272.summary: Separable tokens help organize and structure interfaces by visually dividing regions of a screen, sections of content, or groups of related information. Using separable tokens consistently makes complex layouts easier to navigate and helps users focus on what matters most.

273.title: Shadow
273.summary: Shadow creates the perception of depth and distance between layers, establishing a visual hierarchy that enhances comprehension and adds realism to distinguish between different content layers.

274.title: Size
274.summary: Size defines the height and width of components within the design system, ensuring consistent and harmonious design across applications. It refers to the specific dimensions allocated to elements to maintain uniformity and balance. By controlling these dimensions, Salt provides a structured framework that supports visual consistency and functionality.

275.title: Skip link
275.summary: When focus moves into the webpage, places focus on the skip link.

276.title: Skip link
276.summary: Skip links stay hidden ensuring they aren’t intrusive until accessed through keyboard navigation. Once activated, skip links shift focus to the main content of the web application and hide again.

278.title: Skip link
278.summary: Skip links should be the first focusable element, placed in the screen’s top-left corner. This allows keyboard and screen reader users to easily bypass headers and reach the main content. For more details, see the App header anatomy.

279.title: Slider
279.summary: If focus is outside slider, moves focus to the slider indicator within the tabbing order.

280.title: Slider
280.summary: Selection of a single value from a Slider track. A tooltip displays the value of the Slider "thumb" when the thumb is focused or hovered.

282.title: Slider
282.summary: When selecting a single value, range of numeric values or relative scale.

283.title: Spacing
283.summary: Spacing is a key tool for positioning elements in relation to each other, highlighting some while downplaying others. Consistent spacing boosts visual appeal and guides users through content. It connects size and visual consistency through aligning baselines, gutters, padding, and margins.

284.title: Spinner
284.summary: Improve accessibility by customizing the aria-label to provide additional context about what is loading, for example, aria-label="loading settings panel".

285.title: Spinner
285.summary: The small spinner is used for embedding in individual components (e.g., button or input) that require dynamic loading experiences.

287.title: Spinner
287.summary: To indicate that content is loading and reassure the user that the system is still working.

288.title: Split button
288.summary: A split button enables users to perform a main action and access relevant, supplementary actions inside a menu.

289.title: Split layout
289.summary: When building a sub-section of a page using a SplitLayout, apply semantic HTML. This means using the correct HTML elements for their intended purpose as much as possible.

290.title: Split layout
290.summary: Split layouts display items horizontally at either end of the container by default with its items aligned centrally in the layout.

292.title: Split layout
292.summary: If you need two defined areas at the opposite horizontal ends of a container, for example, if you need two button bar components in a header.

293.title: Splitter
293.summary: Moves a vertical splitter to the left.

294.title: Splitter
294.summary: Applies the default look when applying the Salt theme.

296.title: Splitter
296.summary: Make sure to install the React Resizable Panels package, react-resizable-panels.

297.title: Stack layout
297.summary: When building a subsection of a page using StackLayout, apply semantic HTML. This means using the correct HTML elements for their intended purpose as much as possible.

298.title: Stack layout
298.summary: By default, StackLayout displays items in a single column aligned to the start of the layout.

300.title: Stack layout
300.summary: When you need a layout that's consistently horizontal or vertical. If there isn't enough space in the main axis, scrolling the content is acceptable.

301.title: Static list
301.summary: You must check and test any focusable elements inside the static list content accordingly.

302.title: Static list
302.summary: The default Static list allows users to show non-interactive list items.

304.title: Static list
304.summary: To present a set of static list items. It can be used with a FileDropZone to show the list of files added. It can also be used to create a shopping cart list.

305.title: Status characteristic
305.summary: Statuses provide visual cues that communicate the current state of a system or process. Each status—error, info, caution, and success—helps users quickly understand what’s happening, identify issues, and determine if action is needed. Consistent use of status tokens ensures users can respond confidently and efficiently to changes or events within your application.

306.title: Status indicator
306.summary: Exclude decorative status indicators (status indicators that repeat the information already expressed by the accompanied text) from the screen reader to avoid repetition. If you're adding a status indicator for decorative purposes, pass aria-hidden=”true” to exclude its label from the screen reader.

307.title: Status indicator
307.summary: Use the status prop to change the displayed status. This will affect both the icon and the color of StatusIndicator. The status indicator offers four severity levels that set a distinctive indicator and color.

309.title: Status indicator
309.summary: Where possible, we recommend using a Salt component that uses StatusIndicator, such as Banner, Toast or Tooltip, instead of using StatusIndicator directly.

310.title: Stepper
310.summary: Improve accessibility by customizing the aria-label prop to provide additional context. For example:

311.title: Stepper
311.summary: The Step component's appearance depends on its stage and status props.

313.title: Stepper
313.summary: When there are separate steps within a process, such as a wizard or a multi-step form.

314.title: Support and contributions
314.summary: Help us shape the future of Salt by contributing not just code—but also your thoughts, requests, frustrations and successes.

315.title: Supported platforms
315.summary: Salt supports the latest, stable releases of all major browsers and platforms.

316.title: Switch
316.summary: If focus is on the previous element in the tab order, Tab moves focus to the switch.

317.title: Switch
317.summary: By default, the switch thumb sits to the left side of the track and is in an unchecked state.

319.title: Switch
319.summary: To present an instantaneous, binary choice between two options that doesn’t require the user to submit or confirm the action. The corresponding action takes effect immediately.

320.title: System status
320.summary: By default, the SystemStatus component has the role "status". This means a screen reader will announce the message at the next available opportunity.

321.title: System status
321.summary: Use the info system status to communicate important updates or new features that do not require immediate action.

323.title: System status
323.summary: The primary purpose of the system status is to provide information and, if necessary, prompt further action.

324.title: Table
324.summary: **Provide an accessible name for the Table** - Use a element (preferred method) or apply aria-labelledby / aria-label attributes to the table - The caption should clearly describe the table's content and purpose **Example:**

325.title: Table
325.summary: The table component is used to display tabular data in a structured format. All table elements are supported (, , , etc.).

327.title: Table
327.summary: Only use the Table component for when you need to present simple data.

328.title: Tableau
328.summary: Tableau is a data visualization tool. It allows users to create customized dashboards for business information analytics.

329.title: Tabs
329.summary: You need to check and test any focusable elements included in the tab content.

330.title: Tabs
330.summary: Two different appearances are available for tabs: Bordered and Transparent.

332.title: Tabs
332.summary: Use tabs to organize logically related but mutually exclusive content on a single page.

333.title: Tag
333.summary: When implementing tags to categorize content, ensure color isn't used as the only visual means of conveying information WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Color. Text labels and/or icons should be the primary indicators for differentiating between tag categories, with color serving as a secondary, complementary indicator.

334.title: Tag
334.summary: Tag has two variants: primary and secondary. The primary variant is set by default. Set to secondary with variant=”secondary”.

336.title: Tag
336.summary: For displaying categories in a catalogue or within a group.

337.title: Text
337.summary: We're letting you decide on the user experience you'd like to implement for text. However, you need to remain ADA compliant and provide the correct visual and auditory experience for text truncation. Truncated text must comply with WCAG SC 1.4.4.

338.title: Text
338.summary: Text supports these sets of styles: - Display - Headings - Body - Label - Code These alternative components display text in commonly used styles. Where relevant, use them instead of Text to simplify syntax: - Display1 - Display2 - Display3 - H1 - H2 - H3 - H4 - Label - Code - TextNotation - TextAction

340.title: Text
340.summary: Read more on our typography foundation page.

341.title: Themes
341.summary: A theme is a collection of design tokens that define the overall look and feel of an interface. Themes allow you to quickly switch the visual style of components to match different brands or user preferences, ensuring consistency across your application.

342.title: Toast
342.summary: You must check and test any focusable elements inside the toast content accordingly.

343.title: Toast
343.summary: Use a toast without a status when you need to display general information in a neutral tone.

345.title: Toast
345.summary: To notify users of an event that’s occurred in a peripheral application or workflow. The user should notice the toasts without disrupting their experience or requiring immediate action.

346.title: Toggle button
346.summary: When a toggle button has both an icon and text, use aria-hidden on the icon so that screen readers don't announce its text.

347.title: Toggle button
347.summary: A ToggleButtonGroup allows users to make a single selection from a set of related commands, with only one option selected at a time.

349.title: Toggle button
349.summary: To make a single selection when switching between opposing yet mutually exclusive options.

350.title: Tokenized input
350.summary: Wrap the component in FormField to provide the field with a visible label, help text and a status message for validation feedback. This will ensure it complies with accessibility guidelines. You can find more information in the W3C form instructions.

351.title: Tokenized input
351.summary: The default component has no text input constraints, so you can use it to accept any alphanumeric character or symbol. When the user enters a text value followed by a delimiter, the value is tokenized into a pill.

353.title: Tokenized input
353.summary: The component is typically used in a form. It’s ideal for fields that can contain multiple, specific values related to a single topic or context—and these values can be removed quickly and in their entirety. You would use the component, for example, in a field for email addresses or a fast field for a cash ticket.

354.title: Tooltip
354.summary: Keep the use of tooltips to a minimum and use only when providing extra (non-essential) information for the user.

355.title: Tooltip
355.summary: By default, Tooltip displays a message and an arrow pointing to the relevant UI element. Its default placement is "right," and appears after 300 milliseconds. Use the content prop to pass a simple string to display in the tooltip.

357.title: Tooltip
357.summary: When you want to display a brief message to the user that provides additional information about an interactive UI element.

358.title: Tree
358.summary: Provide an accessible name for the tree using aria-label or aria-labelledby.

359.title: Tree
359.summary: The default Tree displays a collapsible hierarchy with single selection. Click a node to select it, or click the expand icon to reveal child nodes.

361.title: Tree
361.summary: Tree uses a composition model using TreeNode components within a Tree component to define hierarchy.

362.title: Typography
362.summary: Typography refers to the predefined typographic styles that guide the presentation of written language. Typography is essential for improving readability, creating a clear hierarchy, and establishing a visual tone, all of which contribute to more effective and expressive communication. Each text style in Salt includes a font family, font size, line height and font weight. The specific values for each is dependent on the applied theme.

363.title: Vertical navigation
363.summary: Display only links that the user can access.

364.title: Vertical navigation
364.summary: VerticalNavigation supports two appearances: indicator and bordered.

366.title: Vertical navigation
366.summary: For further details on how to use the component to provide navigation, see the navigation pattern

367.title: Vertical navigation
367.summary: Vertical navigation provides users with a structured and intuitive way to navigate different pages, sections or features of your website or application. It's often on the left of the viewport and organizes links into a single or multilevel structure.

368.title: Wizard
368.summary: The wizard allows a workflow-based task to be displayed in a sequence of manageable steps, for easier completion.

369.title: Z-Index
369.summary: Z-index is a CSS property that controls how elements stack on top of each other. The stack order is defined by an element with a higher z-index appearing on top of an element with a lower z-index.
